title: Pre-Shipment Inspection (PSI) and Compliance
summary: The concept of importer responsibility evolved from mandatory PSI requirements to a more nuanced framework involving fee structures, dispute settlement, and eventually shifting towards risk management and post-clearance audit systems.

evolution.policy_model: From mandatory third-party inspection (PSI) to risk-based automated selectivity and post-clearance audit.
evolution.procedure: Transitioned from manual L/C-based inspection to electronic risk management and audit-based compliance.

timeline.change: Defined specific responsibilities for importers under the PSI system.
Introduced a tiered fee structure for importers to pay PSI agencies based on CIF value.
Shifted focus from pre-shipment to post-clearance audit (PCA) and risk-based selection criteria for importers.
Formalized selectivity criteria (Red, Yellow, Blue, Green lanes) for risk management.

Pre-shipment Inspection: The regulations governing the responsibilities of importers under the pre-shipment inspection system have been updated and replaced in their entirety.
Importers are required to specify their chosen inspection agency when opening a Letter of Credit for goods subject to pre-shipment inspection.

Importers must remain informed about inspection procedures by coordinating with the National Board of Revenue, local inspection offices, or the Federation of Bangladesh Chambers of Commerce and Industry.
In the event of a dispute regarding inspection certification, importers are legally required to adhere to the existing laws and regulatory frameworks.
National Board of Revenue: The National Board of Revenue serves as a primary point of contact for importers to obtain necessary information regarding the procedures for pre-shipment inspection of imported goods.
Federation of Bangladesh Chambers of Com: The Federation of Bangladesh Chambers of Commerce and Industry is identified as an organization that importers should consult to clarify and understand the mandatory pre-shipment inspection requirements.

Pre-shipment Inspection: Federation of Bangladesh Chambers of Commerce and Industry
Federation of Bangladesh Chambers of Com: Federation of Bangladesh Chambers of Commerce and Industry

Customs Act 1969: Section 25A of the Act empowers the Government to amend rules related to pre-shipment inspection processes.
Pre-Shipment Inspection Rules 2002: These rules are amended to include specific fee structures for inspection agencies and to update the requirements for training and investigation schedules listed in the appendix.
Pre-shipment Inspection: The rules prescribe a tiered fee structure for inspection agencies based on the CIF value of the imported goods consignment.
An additional fee is applicable for each container sealed during the inspection process.
Importers are prohibited from splitting consignments under a single Letter of Credit to claim lower inspection fees when partial shipment conditions are not applicable.
Customs Valuation: Training courses on valuation techniques are provided for customs officers, with specific programs scheduled for both foreign and local locations.
Customs Audit: Training on post-clearance audit techniques is mandated for customs officers, covering both local and foreign training environments.
Customs Investigation: The rules specify requirements for investigation-related activities for customs officers as part of the official training and operational curriculum.

Customs Post Clearance Audit: This process involves the review of information and documentation provided by importers, exporters, or customs agents. All data collected during this procedure is treated as sensitive information.
Customs Act 1969: Section 204B of this Act mandates that the confidentiality of sensitive information and documents provided for official customs audit purposes must be strictly maintained.

member_objects.resolved_text: ৩.২.১ ট্র্যানজ্যাকশন বেইজড ডেস্ক অডিট—ট্র্যানজ্যাকশন বেইজড ডেস্ক অডিট হলো অপেক্ষাকৃত কম ঝুঁকিপূর্ণ এক বা একাধিক চালানের ক্ষেত্রে পরিচালিত অডিট যা সংশ্লিষ্ট আমদানিকারক/রপ্তানিকারক এবং অন্যান্য সংশ্লিষ্টদের সাথে লিখিত বা টেলিফোন যোগাযোগের মাধ্যমে সম্পাদিত হয়। যদি কোন পণ্যচালানের মূল্য নির্ধারণ, শ্রেণিবিন্যাস সংক্রান্ত বিষয় অথবা সুনির্দিষ্ট অন্যকোন বিষয়ে অধিকতর যাচাই/স্পষ্টীকরণের প্রয়োজন হয়, তাহলে সংশ্লিষ্ট কাস্টম হাউস/কাস্টমস এক্সাইজ ও ভ্যাট কমিশনারেটে দায়িত্বরত কাস্টমস কর্মকর্তা সে পণ্যচালানটিকে ডেস্ক অডিটের জন্য স্ব-স্ব পিসিএ ইউনিটে প্রেরণ করতে পারবেন।

Transaction Based Audit: A transaction-based desk audit is an audit mechanism applied to low-risk cargo shipments. It is conducted through written or telephonic communication with importers, exporters, and other relevant stakeholders.

Customs officers stationed at customs houses or customs, excise, and VAT commissionerates have the authority to refer a shipment to their respective post-clearance audit units for a desk audit if valuation, classification, or other specific matters require further verification or clarification.
Post-Clearance Audit Unit: This unit serves as the designated department where customs officers refer shipments for a transaction-based desk audit to resolve valuation or classification uncertainties.
Appropriate Officer of Customs: Officers assigned to customs houses or customs, excise, and VAT commissionerates are responsible for identifying the need for further verification of shipments and initiating the desk audit process.

Transaction Based Audit: This standing order provides the criteria and indicators for selecting consignments for transaction-based audits to manage customs risk effectively.
The selection strategy focuses on identifying high-risk transactions based on importer/exporter behavior, transaction values, duty rates, country of origin, and discrepancies in manifest data.
Importer and Exporter: Audit selection criteria consider the frequency and history of importers or exporters.

Operational focus is placed on irregular traders, those frequently providing false declarations, one-time traders, first-time traders, or those importing multiple products under various HS Codes in a single consignment.
H.S. Code: Discrepancies in HS Code usage, such as misclassification of accessories as primary machinery or selecting codes inconsistent with the business nature, are key indicators for audit selection.
Abnormal import volumes under specific codes that do not match market statistics or intentional switching of codes following duty rate changes are flagged as high risk.
Customs Duty: Transactions involving high or low customs duty rates are monitored for risks of revenue leakage or fraudulent classification.
Special attention is required for high-duty items where errors could lead to significant revenue loss, and for zero-rated items susceptible to misclassification to gain improper benefits.
Country of Origin: Misdeclaration of the country of origin is a significant risk factor, particularly for goods subject to quotas or specific import restrictions.
Discrepancies between the declared country of origin and the country of shipment, or importing from restricted sources according to Import Policy Orders, trigger mandatory further verification.
Bill of Lading: The Bill of Lading must be cross-verified against the Import General Manifest to ensure consistency in shipper, consignee, and cargo details.
Declarations of origin and product details in the Bill of Lading are validated as part of the customs audit process to prevent misdeclaration.
Airway Bill: The Airway Bill serves as a critical transport document where declared details such as origin must align with other customs documents to mitigate the risk of fraud.
Import General Manifest: The Import General Manifest submitted by the ship's master or agent is reviewed to compare declarations of product description, value, and quantity against other shipping documents.
Operational checks include verifying the consistency of container details with the provided declarations to ensure accuracy in cargo clearance.

Customs Audit: Before finalizing an audit report, the audit team is required to conduct a meeting with the importer or exporter if physical inspection of the premises was necessary.

The purpose of this meeting is to inform the auditee about audit findings, future audit expectations, corrective actions to avoid repeating errors, subsequent customs actions, report preparation, and the appeals process.
The audit team must record all discussions and observations from the meeting and formally sign the minutes of the meeting on a priority basis.
Importer and Exporter: During the final audit meeting, importers and exporters are provided the opportunity to address and correct any identified discrepancies, faulty interpretations, or factual errors regarding the audit findings.
Importers and exporters are entitled to receive formal information regarding the audit outcomes and are instructed on the procedures for filing an appeal if they disagree with the findings.

Economic Risk: This is defined as risks related to money laundering, terror financing, proceeds of crime, illegal financial activities, evasion of customs duties and taxes, and trans-national organized economic crime.
Customs Act 2023: Referred to as the Act, this is the primary legislation governing these rules.
Yellow Lane: A selectivity lane in the automated system designated for reviewing documents without requiring physical examination of the goods.
Data Analytics: A method involving the collection, examination, audit, cleansing, and modeling of digital or analog data for the purpose of risk identification and decision-making.
Customs Risk Management Commissionerate: An entity established by the National Board of Revenue for the management of customs risks and implementation of risk management strategies.
Green Channel: A designated passage at entry points for arriving passengers who are not carrying goods subject to customs duties or taxes.
Green Lane: A selectivity lane in the automated system where goods are cleared without document verification, physical examination, or other risk mitigation procedures.
Goods Declaration: Refers to manifests, import or export declarations, and any other information regarding goods or passengers submitted by a person or agent to the customs authority.
Declarant: A person or licensed agent responsible for the clearance of goods, who is liable for the accuracy of all information and documents submitted in a declaration.
Risk: Defined as economic risks and the potential for violation of the Act or any other customs-related laws, rules, or orders during the clearance of goods.
Risk Indicator: Specific criteria used to select and identify high-risk goods consignments or passengers.
Risk Identification: The process of identifying and listing potential risk areas based on information obtained from various sources under risk management protocols.
Risk Assessment: The process of determining the impact, intensity, and likelihood of potential risks through the analysis of identified risk areas.
Risk Management: The lawful activities conducted by the Customs Risk Management Commissionerate to identify, analyze, determine, assess, and control risk areas.
Documents: Defined as any information stored in physical, electronic, or any other medium.
Goods: Defined as per the meaning assigned in Section 2(30) of the Customs Act.
Consignment of Goods: Refers to goods imported, exported, transited, transshipped, or stored in a bonded warehouse, following prescribed methods and forms.
Clearance of Goods: The process of releasing goods from the control of customs authorities upon compliance with all necessary legal and procedural requirements.
Release of Goods: The action taken by customs to hand over goods to the appropriate person or agent after completion of assessment and payment of duties and taxes.
Profile: A collection and analysis system for risk indicators related to importers, exporters, agents, passengers, or goods to determine the appropriate lane (red, yellow, green, blue) or channel for clearance.
Person: Defined as per the meaning assigned in Section 2(39) of the Customs Act.
Blue Lane: A selectivity lane in the automated system where goods are cleared without immediate physical or document verification, pending post-clearance audit.
Manifest Data: Data obtained from vehicle and cargo declarations, Advance Passenger Information (API), Passenger Name Record (PNR), and reports related to inward/outward movement, transit, or transshipment.
Passenger: Defined to include both regular passengers and crew members.
Red Channel: A passage for arriving passengers at entry points who are carrying goods subject to customs duties, restricted goods, or prohibited items.
Red Lane: A selectivity lane in the automated system where selected consignments are subject to document verification and mandatory 100% physical examination.
Selectivity: A function performed by the automated system or manually by the Customs Risk Management Commissionerate to assign specific risk mitigation procedures to a consignment based on risk indicators or random selection.
Automated Risk Management System: An automated system operated by the Customs Risk Management Commissionerate that assesses the likelihood of risk for a consignment or passenger by comparing declaration data against predefined risk indicators.

Automated System for Customs Data: The system uses selectivities to determine processing channels for cargo and passengers. It establishes an automated risk management framework to evaluate shipment risks based on pre-defined indicators.

The system classifies consignments into red, yellow, blue, and green lanes, and passengers into red and green channels for customs clearance. It also assigns risk scores based on the degree of similarity to established risk indicators.

It creates profiles for importers, exporters, agents, and passengers to identify potential risks through data processing. The system incorporates historical records, intelligence data, and advanced analytical methods to refine its risk assessment indicators.
Data Analytics: Advanced data analytics, machine learning, and artificial intelligence are utilized to process customs documentation and records. These methodologies serve as the technical foundation for identifying and setting risk indicators within the automated management framework.
Manifest Data: Consignment information and related data are compared against established risk indicators to determine potential security or compliance threats during the customs clearance process.

২৫খ। বাধ্যতামূলক প্রি-শিপমেন্ট ইন্সপেকশন।— আমদানিতব্য পণ্য জাহাজ, উড়োজাহাজে অথবা অন্য কোন যানবাহনে বোঝাই করার পূর্বে অথবা বোঝাই করার সময়ে কোন প্রি-শিপমেন্ট ইন্সপেকশন সংস্থা কর্তৃক পরিদর্শন করানো আমদানিকারকদের জন্য বাধ্যতামূলক :

তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, সরকার, সরকারী গেজেটে প্রজ্ঞাপন দ্বারা, কোন শ্রেণীর আমদানিকারক কর্তৃক কোন পণ্য অথবা পণ্যশ্রেণী অথবা কোন কাস্টমস বন্দর অথবা কাস্টমস স্টেশন অথবা উক্ত বন্দর বা স্টেশনের অন্তর্গত অন্য কোন এলাকা হইতে আমদানিকৃত কোন পণ্যকে বাধ্যতামূলক প্রি-শিপমেন্ট ইন্সপেকশন হইতে অব্যাহতি প্রদান করিতে পারিবে।

Pre-shipment Inspection: It is mandatory for importers to have their goods inspected by a pre-shipment inspection agency before or during the loading of the goods onto a ship, aircraft, or any other mode of transport.

The Government has the authority to issue notifications in the official gazette to exempt specific categories of importers, products, or goods imported through designated customs ports or stations from this mandatory inspection requirement.
